_why: Real pages, as compositions of patterns, that must stay valid.
Every other fixture in this repo is a single pattern, which is why a whole
class of defect reached a live site: a pattern is correct on its own and
wrong beside its neighbours. These recipes are the smallest thing that can
hold the library to a page. Changing a pattern so one of them fails is not
forbidden - it is a decision, and this file is where it has to be made
deliberately rather than discovered by a partner.
Each is a page somebody would plausibly build. Add one whenever a real
build finds a composition worth protecting; do not add every permutation,
because a fixture nobody understands is one that gets deleted the first
time it fails.
A recipe carrying a `composition` block additionally ships as a
pre-assembled page shell under compositions/<name>@<version>/, generated
by ci/compose.py. The block lives HERE, on the recipe, rather than in a
sibling file, so there is exactly one statement of which patterns make a
page: the fixture that must stay valid and the shell agents fetch are the
same list, and neither can drift from the other. Bump `version` when the
pattern list or its order changes - the folder name is the contract a
consumer pinned. Everything else about a shell (slot names, guidance,
pattern versions) is derived from the patterns at generation time and
belongs to no file but theirs.

recipes.why: The photo-led homepage built in round 23. A full-viewport opener is the case the fold check exists for.

A page with its site header on it, which no other recipe has. masthead-nav is a component rather than a section on purpose: the fold check judges the first SECTION, so typing the header as one would quietly take every hero beneath it out of that check. This recipe is what notices.
Opener, how it works, the questions, the ask - the ordinary conversion homepage.
The homepage for a brand with no photography. heading-block is not decoration here: benefit-tiles opens at h3 and says so in its own markup, so without an h2 above it the page skips a heading level.

The photography-led homepage: a cinematic full-screen opener, the sign-up flow as image cards, the questions, the ask. Nearly every live lander leads with imagery; this is the shell for them. Image slots take real material or the library's lib/placeholders/ stand-ins while the brand's photography is still coming.

The editorial photography homepage: the claim held above a wide image band rather than over it, alternating image-and-copy rows carrying the argument, and a photographic close. The image-led variant for a brand whose register is considered rather than cinematic.
State the offer, show the tiers, answer the objection, ask.
The pricing page as a table of criteria rather than a row of tier cards - the shape for a brand whose tiers differ on many small things rather than on one headline number.
The pricing page that argues before it prices: the case for paying, then the tiers, then the marks that say the brand is legitimate. For a brand whose price needs a reason first.
On a dating brand this is a conversion page in disguise, so it closes like one.

The safety page written as an explanation rather than a grid - prose, then what happens step by step, then the compliance marks. For a brand whose protections are a process rather than a list of features.
The long safety page: the promises set large, then every protection categorised, then the policies themselves as real links. For a brand with the material to be specific.
The whole of an article: its header and its body.
The ordinary advice article: the summary a reader gets without reading, the piece, where its figures came from, and who wrote it. The default shape for editorial on a dating brand.

The long read: contents at the top so a phone can navigate it, the writing broken part-way by one line lifted out of it, and the writer named at the foot. Two runs of body copy, because a line lifted out of the text has to have text on both sides of it. For a piece past about fifteen hundred words.

The illustrated guide: takeaways at the top, then the writing with a captioned picture set inside it rather than after it, and who wrote it at the foot. The shape for a how-to a reader arrives at with one question and needs shown as well as told.
A one-screen landing page. Nothing below the fold, so the fold is the entire page.

The index of a brand's writing: a stated opener, the pieces as ruled rows rather than a grid of cards, and the topics as plain links. No photography anywhere, because an index rarely has one image per entry that is worth having.

What the brand actually does, as a page: the claim, the feature panels climbing the ground ladder, a table comparing what each tier includes, and the questions that follow. The page a partner asks for when the homepage cannot carry every capability.

A page for one place, and the first shell whose main block is written by the platform rather than by the page. The prose above the members is the part no competitor can copy and the part an agent cannot invent; source-note under the grid is where the honest caveat about what the block shows goes; link-cluster carries the sibling places, which is what stops a set of these reading as isolated doorways.

The index above a set of location pages. Rows rather than cards, because a place has no photograph of its own that is honest to use, and because the set grows: a brand adds a region and adds a row. It exists so a set of location pages is a structure with a parent rather than a run of pages reachable only from a search result.

The paid campaign page: the header carries no menu, so every link on the page is one the page chose; the split opener, the reasons as tiles under the h2 heading-block supplies (benefit-tiles opens at h3 and says so in its own markup), three real voices, the ask. For traffic that arrived from an advert with one promise in mind.
The one-promise campaign page, for a brand with no photograph worth leading with: the claim stated on the brand colour under a menu-free header, the reasons as tiles, three real voices, the ask.

The founder page: a plain statement of who is behind the brand, the person and their story with the portrait given room, the promises the story earns set large, the ask. The page every small brand has and the one a narrative shape was made for.

The about page led by what the brand stands for: the promises before the person, then the founder and their story as the evidence for them. For a brand whose values are the point and whose founder is the proof.
